title: I missed the football managers I grew up with, so I spent 100 days building one with AI
author: king_fredo
selftext:
Let's label this "self promotion" but I want to show around my project and workflow and you might like the story behind the game if you like long reads. Earlier this year, I used Claude to rebuild my local football club’s website. The old one must have been published in 1998 and then carefully avoided touching it while also not maintaining or updating their php4.# forms that must have stopped working years ago. A few hours spread over a couple of days later, there was a new website.

That gave me an idea which has since consumed considerably more than a couple of days.

I grew up with *Anstoss* and *Bundesliga Manager Professional*, (as they are called here in Germany). I missed that kind of football manager: the presentation, personality, the feeling that you were running a club rather than maintaining a particularly demanding spreadsheet.

So I started making one. It’s called **HALFTIME Manager**, it’s been in Early Access on Steam since August 14, and full release is planned for November 1.



My background is business informatics and project management, including IT projects. I have written production code, but I wouldn’t describe myself as a programmer. Planning things, testing them and asking why they don’t work as agreed is much closer to my natural habitat.

Claude Code wrote most of the code. For the last two months, I also used Codex on feature branches; 484 of the 2,911 commits are co-authored by Codex. The soundtrack is 39 tracks made with Suno.

I made the product decisions, played the builds, found things that looked wrong and tried to explain what I actually wanted, later learned to ask for mockups.

The game ships with fictional clubs and players. Steam Workshop lets people bring their own worlds, clubs and leagues. And yes, I want it to sell. This is a game I want people to enjoy, and a commercial project.

The first commit, on July 1, was already a playable MVP. By the second day there were two leagues, promotion and relegation, a cup, training and local hotseat multiplayer. That early pace was quite something. You could ask for a whole system and have something to play with the same day.

By October, I was dealing with foot sliding in animation clips. There are many ways to spend a hundred days. Probably the biggest detour was the match presentation. For eleven weeks, I worked on a Canvas 2D view. It started with a pitch seen from above and gradually acquired stands, floodlight towers, weather, crowds, walking animations and a custom inverse-kinematics rig. There were eighteen face variants. A fairly substantial little world had accumulated around those footballers.

Getting it to run well took a lot of work. Offscreen Canvas was slower in our measurements: 55 ms versus 31 ms for a plain canvas. Caching the crowd brought one measured frame time down from 33.7 to 12.8 ms. There was a lot of measuring, changing something and measuring again.

On September 21, I added a switchable Three.js renderer. On the morning of September 22, the decision was to keep 2D as a fallback. By the end of that day, I had decided to delete it.

The current version has a 3D stadium, player models, motion-capture animations, broadcast cameras, replays, floodlights, walkouts and penalty shootouts.

It also runs faster in my comparison. With the same save on the same machine:

* **Old SVG 2D version:** 28–35 ms per frame, roughly 30 fps.
* **Current Three.js 3D version:** 13.9 ms per frame, roughly 72 fps.

I wish I had gotten rid of the 2D renderer sooner, but it was around septemberish time that Reddit was flooded with Three.js oneshot demos by Fable and Astra. I certainly hadn’t expected the more elaborate-looking version to be the faster one.

Crucially, I didn’t throw away eleven weeks of match simulation. Simulation and rendering had been separated back in July, so the new presentation uses the same deterministic match engine.



Some other things did get thrown away completely:

* Procedural crowd noise. It produced noise. Its claim to being a crowd was less convincing.
* An entire research system: 5,853 lines removed and replaced with the Merch Lab.
* A lot of systems that have now been redone 2 or 3 times.

Since this is a post about building with AI, here are the numbers. These are from my repository and local usage logs, with the estimates marked.

|July|August|September|October 1–9|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Commits|568|895|963|485|
|Commits co-authored by Codex|0|2|240|242|
|Game code, excluding tests and tools|29k lines|83k|125k|135k|
|Claude tokens|\~10B, estimated|15.5B|15.7B|5.0B|
|Output tokens|Not logged|30.7M|28.3M|10.1M|
|Equivalent at API list prices|\~$6k, estimated|$10.5k|$6.9k|$1.4k|

The whole codebase is about 246,000 lines oh which around 135,000 are the game itself; Translations add roughly another 160,000 lines across 29 languages.

The token total needs some explanation before anyone falls off their chair: **36.2 billion measured tokens since August 1, approximately 98% of them cache reads.** Actual output was about 69 million tokens. **The $18,800 API equivalent for August onward is not what I paid.** I used a flat Max 5x subscription, plus two months each of Codex and Suno. I did hit the usage limits. I’m also wary of calling the rising commit count “productivity.”   


What I’ve personally had to get better at is deciding when something is actually finished as the game felt very finished to me end of July, end of September, end of... . At least I can say that the game has matured over time.

I've been working in a technical support team for AMD in 2010 in the UK. I could "remotely" (over the phone with 60 year old Scotsmen) fix computers. I made hundreds of hours technical trainings for clients. I *feel* what is missing or broken. I also learned that something that looks "okay" just isn't - fix that shit. This helps a lot. E.g. unloading geometry and shaders sounds like a useful optimization until you realize they’ll be needed and loaded again a few seconds later. LLMs - at this point - needs human to take it by the hand here but being part of the impressive development of the models in short time, this should be a matter of weeks. I’ve become much more insistent about seeing the result in the game and getting measurements to support performance claims. A confident explanation doesn’t settle it for me anymore.

**Context**. I use a shared project journal, memory notes and rule files, with Cairn and Tokensave (both on Github) helping with continuity and code context. Recording *why* I chose something is especially useful when a later session comes back to the same problem. When I change my mind, the record needs to say which decision replaced the old one. And I need to follow those decisions through. Bits of the abandoned 2D approach kept confusing later sessions. Once I’ve replaced something, leaving half of it lying around creates more work for me later. Apparently “we’re not doing that anymore” also requires some actual tidying.

For visual changes, I now ask for two or three mockups before implementation. It’s much easier for me to choose between concrete options than to describe an exact picture in my head and hope the first result matches it.

Then there are the translations. Translating is a nightmare. Having 29 language packs in the repository is an easily achievable goal. The trick is to translate the context correctly so that a “soccer van” doesn’t become a “Ventalitor.” Right now, a few very efficient Haiku 5.5 agents are running, performing cross-translation and, with more context, doing the whole thing almost from scratch again. Fortunately, the many millions of tokens are extremely cheap.



The part I’m least happy with is **visibility**. After roughly eight weeks of Early Access, sales are in the few hundreds. I’m pleased with where the game is now, so that’s disappointing. There hasn’t been a shortage of material: patch notes, Steam events, artwork, a press kit, localised screenshots, a translated store page and now a third trailer.

I sent keys to creators through Keymailer in Brazil, Spain, France, Austria and the UK. Three creators made videos, seventeen videos in total.

Fifteen came from one Austrian creator who has played for fifty hours.

That particular number means quite a lot to me. Someone found enough in this thing to spend fifty hours with it.

Steam Curator Connect hasn’t been worth the time for me so far. I also haven’t heared back from the press or built social channels. Looking at that list, I can see how much effort I put into preparing material compared with finding ways to get it in front of people.

That’s something I still have to learn. I know how to open the project and start working on the next problem. Getting people interested enough to try the game has been much less straightforward.

At the moment, HALFTIME Manager runs on Windows and Linux, supports 29 languages and local hotseat for up to four managers, and has Steam Workshop support for worlds, sponsors, dilemmas and themes.

[HALFTIME Manager on Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5005920/HALFTIME_Manager/)

If you make videos about football games, write about them or know a community that might enjoy this, I’d be happy to hear from you. Yesterday, local computer press wrote about some [Chineese guys that "made GTA with 10k$ of token-use"](https://www.computerbase.de/news/gaming/ki-statt-entwicklerteam-taipei-gta-verschlingt-10-000-dollar-an-ki-tokens.99674/). HTM is a success story: I spent **18k$** worth of token on soccer manager. My game also looks better - even the city surrounding the stadium - give me some coverage!

And for anyone here who has released an AI-assisted game: **what actually helped people discover it?**

Happy to answer questions about the workflow, the numbers or the short life of the 2D fallback.

replies.author: king_fredo
replies.body:
On Football Manager - I’m not trying to out-depth FM. A lot of players love it, but many also say it feels like work, like running a spreadsheet. HALFTIME goes the other way, with a more arcade-style approach. The goal is that you can take a third-division club into Europe in a few hours, not a few hundred. Every decision should feel like playing, not like admin.

Matchdays are 3D TV broadcasts in a stadium you expand step by step yourself, with crowd, floodlights and weather, which - I feel - also looks a bit nicer. It’s a solo project, runs natively on Linux/SteamOS, comes in 29 languages, and there’s no yearly re-release: new features arrive as updates to the game you already own. And I commit to listen to users feedback.

On the stadium: the white cushion skin is a style quite a few modern stadiums share, but the geometry is not a copy. Every stand gets its own shell that grows as you expand it, with its own height and its own ends. In the trailer you see a Hamburg FC Club with mainly red color -  The color of the stadium would be different if that club had a different main color. But yes, I get your point.
